prize_parts.citation: For the theory and experimental demonstration of strong coupling between a single artificial atom and a single microwave photon in superconducting circuits (circuit quantum electrodynamics).

statement.case_for: Circuit QED opened a genuinely new regime: a single solid-state artificial atom strongly and controllably coupled to a single microwave photon, with the physics understood in every detail (vacuum Rabi splitting, dispersive shifts, photon-number-resolved readout, quantum non-demolition measurement). The 2004 theory proposal and the 2004 strong-coupling experiment form a clean theory-plus-experiment pair, and the result has been reproduced and extended in dozens of laboratories for twenty years. It is also the shared language of microwave quantum optics, waveguide QED and superconducting processors, so its reach goes well beyond one application. I would ground the citation in the discovery of the strong-coupling regime and its measurement toolbox, not in quantum computing, which is still ahead of us, since fault-tolerant machines do not exist yet and the prize should reward the physics that has already been shown to be robust.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is proximity to the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling and energy quantisation in circuits, which already honoured one pillar of superconducting quantum technology and two of its pioneers (Devoret, Martinis). A committee may reasonably feel that one recognition of this area in consecutive years is enough, or that circuit QED is mostly cavity-QED ideas (recognised in 2012 with Haroche) transplanted to a chip, with the transmon and other engineering steps responsible for much of the practical success. There is also an attribution gap: Girvin and Huang were on the 2004 theory proposal and Yale colleagues were part of the experiment, but they are outside the credited names, and a three-name limit cannot capture all of this fairly.

responses.point: Eva Lindroth ranked the optical lattice clock (B047) first as a clean precision-measurement advance where theory and experiment agree quantitatively, with timely prospects for redefining the second, and she placed circuit QED fourth with concern about overlap with 2025.
responses.response: I agree with her on the quality of the lattice-clock work: a 1e-18 regime, reproduced across many laboratories, is exactly the robustness I look for, and I rank B047 sixth only because I weigh the discovery content differently, not because I doubt the science. My reservation is that the clock's fundamental-physics payoff so far is upper limits on constants and dark matter, and it follows two earlier metrology prizes (2005 combs, 2012 ion control), so it reads as a refinement of an honoured toolbox. Circuit QED, in contrast, opened a regime that did not exist before 2004. On the overlap with 2025 I disagree that it is too close: macroscopic tunnelling and energy quantisation in a circuit is a different phenomenon from strong light-matter coupling at the single-photon level, and the second does not follow from the first. I would keep B047 as a strong alternative if the committee prefers metrology.

responses.point: Olle Eriksson ranked twisted bilayer graphene (B017) first for its theory-experiment loop and tunable platform, and placed circuit QED fourth, noting that the 2025 prize and Devoret's Yale links may complicate the narrative.
responses.response: I share his appreciation for the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 experiment, and I ranked B017 third. Where I differ is maturity: the pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is unresolved and twist-angle disorder still limits quantitative comparison between devices, so I am more cautious than he is about whether the central physical picture is settled. On his concern about Devoret, I accept it as a real narrative problem, but the credited trio contains no 2025 laureate and the 2004 work stands on its own as the discovery of a new coupling regime. The attribution point is fair: the Kane-style question of who is missing exists here too (Girvin, Huang), and I would not hide it.

responses.point: Bernhard Mehlig ranked topological insulators (B006) first for conceptual reach, a sharp prediction followed by a decisive transport experiment, and a good fit with earlier topological-phase prizes, while admitting the cut to three names is contested.
responses.response: The conceptual case is strong and I accept that this is the kind of clean prediction-then-experiment story the committee values; I ranked it only seventh because it is outside my field and I defer to condensed-matter colleagues. My substantive worry is about whether the allocation can be made fair: dropping Mele from the Kane-Mele pair, as he and several colleagues propose, seems hard to defend, while including him forces out Molenkamp or Hasan and loses an experimental leg, and the HgTe proposal of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is outside the credited names. I also think the 2016 topological-phases prize makes novelty arguments harder than he suggests. If the committee can settle the allocation, I would not oppose it, and I list it below circuit QED only on the attribution and overlap issues.

responses.point: Mark Pearce ranked the IceCube high-energy neutrino discovery (B048) first as a detector many doubted could work, with a confirmed diffuse flux and growing source associations, while noting the credit problem within a large collaboration.
responses.response: I defer to him and others on astroparticle physics, and I agree that the diffuse flux detection is a real and well-confirmed new observation. My qualification is that he himself says source identification rests on a few objects, and I would want the citation to rest only on what has been reproduced independently, for instance by KM3NeT. I would also ask how a two-person prize captures the leadership of a collaboration of hundreds, but I cannot judge that fairly from my position. It is a serious candidate and I do not claim circuit QED is better on scientific merit alone, only that its robustness across many independent laboratories is greater than that of the source-identification part of IceCube.

responses.point: Stefan Kroll ranked the optical lattice clock first as an advance that extended the reach of experiment, and ranked circuit QED fifth for its method and platform value but flagged overlap with 2025 and the missing Girvin and Huang credit.
responses.response: I take his criticism that circuit QED is partly a method and a platform seriously, and it is why I would word the citation around the discovery of the strong-coupling regime rather than the architecture. I think it is more than a method: dispersive readout and quantum non-demolition measurement of an artificial atom are physics results that did not exist before. I agree on the Girvin and Huang gap, and I think the committee should discuss it openly instead of assuming that three names are enough.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges circuit QED sufficiently distinct from the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, or prefers to wait.
Whether the three-name limit can fairly represent the 2004 theory and experiment given the omission of Girvin, Huang and other Yale contributors.
Whether the discovery is best framed as the strong-coupling regime or the broader readout and architecture toolbox, which affects the citation and the credit between Blais and the experimentalists.
Whether the optomechanics case (B007) can be resolved with three of five strong names, since I proposed Teufel, Aspelmeyer and Kippenberg while Eva Lindroth proposed Cleland instead of Teufel.
statement.conflict_note: Possible conflict: I am a theorist in superconducting circuits at Chalmers and director of WACQT, the Swedish quantum-computing programme that depends directly on the circuit QED architecture, and I know the community, including Wallraff and Schoelkopf as scientific peers, and Chalmers has hosted and collaborated with 2025 laureates. I do not know of a personal collaboration or institutional tie with the three credited names, but the committee should consider whether my ranking B038 first requires recusal or discounting, and I accept that.
